stages.title: Advanced climatology
stages.hook: Why would Earth be about 33 °C colder with an atmosphere that only lets in sunlight and does not slow heat leaving?
explain: The simplest climate model balances energy. Earth intercepts sunlight over a disc of area πR² but has a surface of 4πR², so average incoming solar energy per square metre is S₀/4. With S₀ ≈ 1361 W/m² and planetary albedo α ≈ 0.30, absorbed energy is S₀(1 − α)/4 ≈ 238 W/m².

A blackbody radiating 238 W/m² has temperature T = (238 ÷ σ)^¼, with σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²/K⁴. This gives about 255 K (−18 °C). The observed mean is about 288 K (+15 °C); the difference of about 33 K is the natural greenhouse effect.

The extra forcing from added CO₂ is roughly ΔF = 5.35 ln(C/C₀) W/m². Doubling CO₂ gives about 3.7 W/m². Equilibrium climate sensitivity is the long-term warming for doubled CO₂; the IPCC assesses a likely range of about 2.5 to 4 °C. Feedbacks (water vapour, ice albedo, clouds) amplify or damp the direct response.

Climate also varies through modes such as ENSO, volcanic eruptions (sulfate aerosols cool for a year or two) and orbital cycles over tens of thousands of years (Milankovitch cycles). Separating natural variability from human influence relies on attribution studies comparing models with and without human forcing.

example.q: Calculate the effective radiating temperature if absorbed energy is 238 W/m² and σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²/K⁴.
steps: √ gives about 64,800; √ again gives about 255 K.

analogies.home: A thermos slows heat loss; a blanket raises the temperature you feel without adding heat.
analogies.city: Dark roofs absorb more sunlight; white roofs reflect it, changing local energy balance.
analogies.sea: Oceans store most of the added heat, delaying surface warming.
analogies.tech: Climate models are energy-balance equations solved on a three-dimensional grid.

stages.mnemonic: In minus out sets the temperature: S₀(1−α)/4.

misc.wrong: Because CO₂ is only a tiny fraction of the air, it cannot affect climate.
misc.right: Radiative effect depends on absorption properties, not volume share; trace gases like CO₂ strongly absorb infrared.

stages.limits: Cloud feedbacks remain the biggest uncertainty in sensitivity estimates; ranges, not single values, are reported.

stages.title: Environmental change and sustainability
stages.hook: If every person on Earth lived like the average person in your country, how many Earths would we need?
explain: Environmental change includes climate change, land-use change, biodiversity loss, pollution and freshwater stress. The planetary boundaries framework identifies limits within which humanity can operate safely, including climate, biosphere integrity, land use, freshwater, nitrogen and phosphorus cycles, and ocean acidification.

Sustainability balances environmental, social and economic needs. The 2015 UN Sustainable Development Goals set 17 goals. The IPAT identity, Impact = Population × Affluence × Technology, shows that impact depends on how many people, how much each consumes and how efficiently resources are used.

Ecological footprint compares human demand with the biosphere's regenerative capacity (biocapacity), both measured in global hectares. Footprints vary widely: per-person consumption in high-income countries is several times that of low-income countries, while total impact depends also on population.

Mitigation reduces emissions or enhances sinks; adaptation adjusts to impacts. Tools include renewable energy, efficiency, nature-based solutions such as mangrove restoration, carbon pricing and circular economy design. Trade-offs matter: biofuel crops can compete with food, and dams affect river ecosystems and communities.

example.q: Impact = P × A × T. A country doubles population, keeps per-person consumption the same, and halves resource use per unit consumed (T). What happens to total impact?

analogies.home: A household budget: income equals biocapacity, spending equals footprint.
analogies.farm: Agroforestry combines crops and trees to protect soil and store carbon.
analogies.city: Cities cut footprints by compact design, public transport and efficient buildings.
analogies.tech: Satellite data monitors deforestation and ocean heat.

misc.right: It also includes social equity and economic wellbeing; the three are linked.

stages.title: Population modelling
stages.hook: The world's population grew from 1 billion around 1800 to over 8 billion in 2022. Will it keep growing forever?
explain: Demography models population by births, deaths and migration. Crude birth rate (CBR) and crude death rate (CDR) are per 1,000 people per year. Natural increase = (CBR − CDR) ÷ 10, expressed as a percentage. Total fertility rate (TFR) is the average number of children per woman; replacement level is about 2.1 in low-mortality countries.

Exponential growth follows N(t) = N₀e^(rt), with doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ (growth rate in percent) years. Real populations show logistic or other patterns when constraints apply, but human populations mainly change through falling fertility rather than a fixed carrying capacity.

The demographic transition model describes shifts from high birth and death rates (stage 1) through falling death rates and rapid growth (stage 2), falling birth rates (stage 3), and low rates (stage 4), with possible decline (stage 5). Age-sex pyramids show structure: wide bases mean young populations; narrow bases mean ageing. Population momentum means growth continues for decades after fertility falls because many young adults reach childbearing age.

The dependency ratio compares dependents (under 15 and over 64) with the working-age population (15–64). Projections, such as those from the United Nations, use scenarios; most show global population peaking later this century, but regional paths differ greatly.

example.q: A population grows at 2 percent a year. Estimate its doubling time.
steps: Use the rule of 70: doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ r.

analogies.city: Ageing cities need more care services, younger ones need schools.

stages.title: Urban systems and spatial planning
stages.hook: Why do cities in many countries show one very large city and then a steady drop in size?
explain: Urban systems are networks of cities linked by flows of people, goods and information. The rank-size rule says the nth largest city has about 1/n the population of the largest. Some countries fit this; others have a primate city that is far larger than the next (for instance Bangkok in Thailand, or Paris in France).

Central place theory (Walter Christaller) explains hierarchies of settlements: small places offer low-order goods bought often; larger centres offer high-order goods bought rarely and have bigger market areas. Gravity models predict interaction between two places: I ∝ (P₁ × P₂) ÷ dᵏ, where k is often near 2.

Spatial planning guides land use, transport and services. Tools include zoning, urban growth boundaries, transit-oriented development and green infrastructure. Compact cities cut travel distances but need affordable housing; sprawl consumes farmland and raises car dependence. Informal settlements house over a billion people worldwide and need upgrading, secure tenure and services rather than only clearance.
Smart-city and 15-minute city ideas aim at reachable daily needs. Planners evaluate accessibility, for example the share of people within 500 m of a bus stop, using GIS network analysis.

example.q: If the largest city has 12 million people, what does the rank-size rule predict for the 4th largest?

analogies.home: Corner shops serve nearby people; a big hospital serves a whole region, like central place hierarchies.
analogies.city: Bus lines meeting at interchanges concentrate flows, like network nodes.
analogies.farm: Market towns in farming regions are spaced so farmers can travel to them in a day.
analogies.tech: Network analysis finds the shortest route and service areas for ambulances.

A settlement providing goods and services to surrounding areas.

stages.title: Economic and regional development
stages.hook: Why do regions that start slightly ahead often pull further ahead, and what can break the cycle?
explain: Regional development differs because of resources, location, history, institutions and investment. Gunnar Myrdal described cumulative causation: advantages such as skilled workers, infrastructure and markets attract more investment, which reinforces the advantage. Backwash effects draw resources from the periphery to the core; spread effects pass benefits outward.

Albert Hirschman argued that growth appears first in some places and spreads through trickle-down. Growth poles, clusters and special economic zones try to seed growth. Industrial clusters, such as Silicon Valley or the Pearl River Delta, gain from shared suppliers, labour and knowledge (agglomeration economies).

Measuring inequality: the Gini coefficient ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person has all). The location quotient LQ = (regional share of an industry) ÷ (national share) shows specialisation: LQ above 1 means the region is more specialised than the nation.

Policies include infrastructure investment, education, regional funds (such as the EU's cohesion funds), trade agreements and decentralisation. Development outcomes depend on governance, not just money. Different paths exist: export-led manufacturing in East Asia, resource-based growth in some economies, services-led growth elsewhere.

example.q: In a region, 20% of jobs are in a certain industry, while nationally only 10% of jobs are in that industry. Find the location quotient.
example.a: LQ = 2, the region is specialised in the industry

analogies.home: A well-stocked kitchen makes cooking easier and attracts guests, as advantages attract more investment.
analogies.city: Tech clusters pull in workers, which attract more firms.
analogies.farm: Co-operatives pool farmers to gain markets and bargaining power.
analogies.tech: Digital infrastructure lets small towns join global markets.

stages.title: Disaster risk and vulnerability mapping
stages.hook: Two cities suffer the same earthquake. One has few deaths and the other thousands. What changed between hazard and disaster?
explain: Natural hazards (earthquakes, floods, cyclones, droughts) become disasters when they hit vulnerable people. A common framework is Risk = Hazard × Exposure × Vulnerability ÷ Capacity. Hazard is the probability and intensity of an event, exposure is who or what is in harm's way, vulnerability is susceptibility to damage, and capacity is the ability to prepare, respond and recover.

Return period T is the average interval between events of a given size: annual probability p = 1/T. The chance of at least one event in n years is 1 − (1 − p)ⁿ. A "100-year flood" has a 1 percent chance each year, and about a 26 percent chance of happening at least once in 30 years.

Vulnerability mapping combines layers: hazard zones, population density, building quality, poverty, age, access to hospitals and evacuation routes. Indices such as a social vulnerability index weight indicators, but weights are subjective and should be tested for sensitivity.

Disaster risk reduction (DRR) includes early warning systems, building codes, land-use planning, ecosystem protection and community preparedness. The Sendai Framework (2015–2030) guides global DRR. Cyclone shelters and warning systems in Bangladesh cut cyclone deaths dramatically over decades, showing that vulnerability can be reduced.

example.q: What is the probability that a 50-year flood occurs at least once in a 10-year period?
steps: Probability of no flood in 10 years = 0.98¹⁰ ≈ 0.817.

analogies.home: A home with smoke alarms and a plan is less vulnerable to a fire than one without.
analogies.city: Buildings with strict codes sway but stand in earthquakes.
analogies.farm: Diverse crops and savings help farmers survive a drought year.
analogies.tech: Satellite rain data feed early warning systems for floods.

stages.mnemonic: Hazard plus people plus weakness, minus preparedness, equals disaster.

stages.title: Geospatial data analysis
stages.hook: A map shows disease cases clustered in one district. How do you decide whether this is real clustering or just chance?
explain: Geospatial data analysis uses statistics tailored to location. The first law of geography (Waldo Tobler, 1970) states that near things are more related than distant things. This spatial autocorrelation violates the independence assumption of many ordinary statistics.

Point pattern analysis compares the observed mean nearest-neighbour distance to the expected distance under randomness: Rn = d_obs ÷ d_exp, with d_exp = 0.5 ÷ √(n/A). Rn near 1 is random, below 1 clustered, above 1 dispersed. Moran's I measures spatial autocorrelation from −1 to +1.

Interpolation estimates values at unsampled places. Inverse distance weighting uses nearby points more; kriging models spatial correlation using a variogram. Correlation of mapped variables is not causation, and ecological fallacy occurs when group-level relationships are wrongly applied to individuals. The modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP) means results change with how areas are drawn.
Good practice: define the question, check data quality and coordinate systems, choose a method, test significance, check sensitivity to scale and boundaries, and present uncertainty.

example.q: 25 points lie in an area of 100 km². The observed mean nearest-neighbour distance is 0.6 km. Is the pattern clustered?
example.a: Rn = 0.6, so the pattern is clustered

analogies.city: Crime or disease mapping looks for hot spots.

stages.title: Land-use modelling
stages.hook: If you know how land was used last decade and why it changes, can you predict the map in 2040?
explain: Land-use models describe and predict how land cover changes. Von Thünen's model of agricultural location shows rent falling with distance from the market. Economic rent R = Y(p − c) − Y·f·d, where Y is yield, p price, c production cost, f transport cost per unit per km and d distance. Land goes to the use with the highest rent at each distance, forming rings of land use.

Markov chain models predict change using a transition matrix of probabilities. If P is the matrix and x₀ the current shares, then x₁ = x₀P. Cellular automata update each cell by neighbours and rules, and agent-based models simulate decisions by farmers, firms and households. Combined models often include suitability layers, constraints (protected areas) and drivers (roads, slope, distance to cities).

Models need calibration (fitting to past data) and validation (testing against independent data). Accuracy metrics include the confusion matrix, overall accuracy and the Kappa coefficient. Scenarios, such as business as usual and strong protection, explore alternatives rather than forecast one future.

Land-use change drives deforestation, urban expansion and loss of habitat. In the Brazilian Amazon, roads and cattle and soy expansion have been major drivers, while protected areas and enforcement have slowed clearing in some periods.

example.q: Today the land is 60% forest and 40% farmland. Each decade, 10% of forest becomes farmland and 20% of farmland becomes forest. What are the shares after one decade?

analogies.home: Rooms in a house are used where they suit: kitchen near the pantry. Land uses where rents are highest.

stages.title: Regional comparative geography
stages.hook: Choose any two continents. What do their physical and human geographies really tell us about how they differ and what they share?
explain: Africa (about 30.4 million km², roughly 1.4 billion people) straddles the equator and has the Sahara, the Congo basin, the Ethiopian Highlands and the Rift Valley. It is the youngest in median age. Asia (about 44.6 million km², over 4.7 billion people) contains Earth's highest mountains, the Tibetan Plateau, monsoon river basins and over half of humanity. Europe (about 10 million km²) is a peninsula-rich continent with a long coastline, dense networks of cities and the European Union as a regional bloc.

North America (about 24.7 million km²) has the Rockies, the Great Plains, the Great Lakes and a mix of high-income and middle-income economies. South America (about 17.8 million km²) has the Andes, the Amazon basin and the Atacama Desert. Oceania (about 8.5 million km² of land, including Australia, New Zealand and Pacific islands) mixes an arid continental interior, a coastal population and thousands of islands vulnerable to sea-level rise. Antarctica (about 14.2 million km²) has an ice sheet over 4 km thick in places, holds about 90 percent of the world's ice, has no permanent residents and is governed by the Antarctic Treaty (1959).

Comparative geography looks for patterns and causes. Relief and climate shape settlement; history, colonialism, trade routes and institutions shape economies; resource distribution shapes trade. Regional integration (EU, ASEAN, African Union, Mercosur) shows different models of cooperation.
Comparison needs care: choose indicators carefully, adjust for scale (per capita, per area) and avoid ranking cultures. Within every continent diversity is huge, and generalisations hide this.

example.q: Asia has about 44.6 million km² and 4.7 billion people. Africa has about 30.4 million km² and 1.4 billion people. Which has the higher population density and what are the densities?
steps: Asia: 4.7 billion ÷ 44.6 million km² ≈ 105 per km².
Asia is more than twice as dense.
example.a: Asia: about 105 per km²; Africa: about 46 per km². Asia is denser
